A0018.title: Identity Authentication (Login)
A0018.definition: Requiring users to confirm their identity through login or similar means when requesting related resources from a terminal.
A0018.description: In most cases, identity authentication takes the form of login. Without verifying login status, it is very difficult to continuously monitor terminal access behavior, because both request characteristics and request sources are trivially easy to forge. This makes evading server-side continuous monitoring of terminal access a common method for avoiding penalties for resource abuse. For this reason, many businesses now use identity authentication as an effective means of achieving continuous monitoring of terminal access behavior. Without authentication, terminals can only access a limited type or quantity of resources; to access more resources, identity authentication is required.
A0018.limitation: The protective effectiveness of identity authentication is heavily dependent on the cost of obtaining a business identity — both the registration cost and the login authentication cost — and is also closely related to the severity of account penalties (A0020). Some websites allow arbitrary bulk registration of user identities, in which case the value of identity authentication is very limited.

A0018-001.title: Zero-Knowledge Proof
A0018-001.definition: A special interactive protocol that allows a prover to prove to a verifier that a statement is true without providing any information about the statement to the verifier.
A0018-001.description: The core idea of zero-knowledge proof is that a prover, through a series of interactions, demonstrates to a verifier that they possess evidence supporting a certain statement, without revealing any information about that evidence during the process. A typical application scenario is identity authentication: the prover can prove to the verifier that they know a certain password without disclosing any information about the password. For example, in e-commerce scenarios, when a user's identity is in doubt, the user can be asked to confirm their identity by selecting previously purchased items; or in social scenarios, when a user's identity is in doubt, the user can be asked to confirm their identity by selecting their own friends.
A0018-001.limitation: The user may lose the ability to judge certain knowledge, leading to verification failure. For normal users who have been inactive for a long time or have vague memories, they may be mistakenly identified as suspicious identities, causing experience and false positive issues. Moreover, once the auxiliary knowledge is obtained by an attacker through social engineering, credential stuffing, or other means, the zero-knowledge proof can also be bypassed.
